content.text: {"answers":[{"id":"p1","answer":"The documentation does not settle this. It shows that `Console.print(*objects, sep=\" \", end=\"\\n\", style=...)` accepts multiple objects and that an internal `_collect_renderables()` step converts each object (strings going through `render_str()` → `Text`) before rendering, and that `sep` defaults to `\" \"`, so the printed content would read \"Hello World!\". But the exact number of renderable objects produced (whether the two strings are merged into one `Text` or kept as two) is not documented, so I cannot state it with confidence."},{"id":"p2","answer":"The documentation describes `Table._extra_width` as a property giving the characters consumed by box edges and dividers [rich/table.py:296-303](), and `_calculate_column_widths(console, options)` as returning per-column widths including padding, using `options.max_width`. However, the concrete numeric values for this particular README table (the value of `_extra_width`, the width handed in, and the resulting width list) are not given anywhere in the documentation, so I cannot provide them."},{"id":"p3","answer":"The documentation describes the detection algorithm in `Console._detect_color_system()` (Jupyter → TRUECOLOR; non-terminal or `TERM=dumb` → None; Windows → WINDOWS/EIGHT_BIT/TRUECOLOR; else `COLORTERM=truecolor|24bit` → TRUECOLOR, otherwise a `TERM`-suffix lookup defaulting to STANDARD), but it does not record what the environment was in this particular run. Without knowing whether the output file was a TTY and what `TERM`/`COLORTERM`/`NO_COLOR`/`FORCE_COLOR` were set to, I cannot say which system was chosen. Note that when the target is not a terminal the color system is `None` and no ANSI color codes are emitted."},{"id":"p4","answer":"The docs state `divide_line(text, width, fold)` in `rich/_wrap.py` \"computes line-break offsets for word wrapping\" and returns a list of break offsets consumed by `Text.divide()`. For \"Hello World!\" at width 100 the text fits on one line, so no break offsets are needed (an empty offset list). At width 11 the string is 12 cells, so a break at the word boundary before \"World!\" would be returned — but the documentation does not spell out the exact offset values or whether a leading 0 is included, so the precise return values are not settled here."},{"id":"p5","answer":"The documentation does not describe distinct styled vs. styleless branches inside `Console.print`. It documents only that `style` is a `StyleType` applied to all output, that objects pass through `_collect_renderables()` → `RenderHook.process_renderables()` → `render()` → `Segment` stream → `_buffer` (and additionally `_record_buffer` when `record=True`). The exact segments for this call are not derivable from the documentation."},{"id":"p6","answer":"The top border comes from the `Box` instance used by the table — by default `box.HEAVY_HEAD` [rich/table.py:162]() — via `Box.get_top(widths)` [rich/box.py:95-113](), after `Box.substitute()` has possibly swapped the box for platform safety. The documentation does not list the literal character set of `HEAVY_HEAD`, so I cannot write out the exact string for widths [14, 35, 19, 16]."},{"id":"p7","answer":"Table cells are rendered as ordinary renderables; a `str` cell is converted by `Console.render_str()`, which applies console markup when markup is enabled (it is by default) and may also apply the highlighter if `Table(highlight=True)` or the column's `highlight` is set. So `[red]...[/red]` would be parsed as a markup tag, producing a `Text` whose plain content is \"Solo: A Star Wars Story\" with a `Span` covering \"Solo\" styled `red`. The documentation does not show the exact span indices, and it does not confirm whether the table passes `markup` through unchanged in every case, so the precise span list is not fully settled."},{"id":"p8","answer":"`export_text()` requires `record=True` and returns the recorded output as plain text with styles removed — it processes the recorded `Segment` stream through `Segment.strip_styles()`, so the result contains no ANSI escape sequences. The documentation does not contain the actual rendered output of this scenario, so I cannot quote its first three lines."},{"id":"g1","answer":"All three export methods require the `Console` to have been constructed with `record=True`; recording populates the thread-safe `_record_buffer` with every rendered `Segment`. Each export method takes a `clear` parameter that defaults to `True`, which discards the recording buffer after export — so a second call without having re-rendered anything returns empty/blank content. The documentation says the methods \"require `record=True`\" but does not state the specific exception type raised when recording was never enabled."},{"id":"g2","answer":"`Console.is_terminal` is `True` if writing to a TTY-capable device, and it respects explicit overrides. The documented influences are: the `force_terminal` constructor argument (explicit override), the `FORCE_COLOR` environment variable (forces `is_terminal` to `True` when set and non-empty), and `TTY_COMPATIBLE` (`\"1\"` forces `True`, `\"0\"` forces `False`). Related variables: `NO_COLOR` disables color, `TERM=dumb`/`unknown` makes `is_dumb_terminal` true and disables color and cursor movement, `COLORTERM=truecolor|24bit` selects truecolor, and `TTY_INTERACTIVE` overrides `is_interactive`. The documentation lists these influences but does not give a definitive precedence ordering among them."},{"id":"g3","answer":"Because `markup=True` is the Console default, any user text containing square-bracket sequences that look like tags is parsed as markup: it can be swallowed/restyled, and mismatched or orphan closing tags raise `MarkupError` (e.g. `[bold]Hello[/red]`, or a `[/]` with nothing open). Metadata tags starting with `@` can also raise if their parameters fail `ast.literal_eval`. The supported fix is `rich.markup.escape(text)`, which backslash-escapes tag-like sequences (and handles trailing backslashes), so `\\[bold]` renders as the literal `[bold]`. You can also disable parsing per call with `markup=False` or on the Console."},{"id":"g4","answer":"If fewer renderables than columns are supplied, the missing cells are filled with `\"\"`. If more renderables are supplied than there are columns, new unnamed columns are created automatically (inheriting `highlight=self.highlight`). A cell value that is neither `None`, a `str`, nor a Rich renderable raises `errors.NotRenderableError`; `None` is allowed and renders as an empty cell."},{"id":"g5","answer":"Box substitution happens at render time in `Box.substitute()`: when `options.legacy_windows` is true and `safe=True`, certain boxes are swapped via `LEGACY_WINDOWS_SUBSTITUTIONS`; and when `options.ascii_only` is true (encoding does not start with \"utf\"), all non-ASCII boxes are replaced with `ASCII`. The legacy-Windows swap can be disabled by passing `safe_box=False` (on the `Table`/`Panel`, or `Console(safe_box=False)`); the ASCII-only substitution is driven by the output encoding rather than by a flag."},{"id":"g6","answer":"The documentation states that `Console(quiet=True)` \"suppresses all output\" / \"suppress all output\", but it does not describe what happens to already-buffered segments, nor does it document any handling of `BrokenPipeError` or `UnicodeEncodeError` during writes. Those behaviours are not settled by the documentation."},{"id":"g7","answer":"`Console.get_style(name, *, default=None)` resolves a style by name from the theme stack (the per-thread `ThemeStack`, whose themes inherit from `DEFAULT_STYLES` unless `inherit=False`), or, failing a named lookup, parses the string as a style definition via `Style.parse`. If the name cannot be resolved and no `default` is supplied, it raises `MissingStyle`. An unparseable style definition string raises `errors.StyleSyntaxError` from `Style.parse`."}]}
